In Lima on 16 November 2024 Biden and Xi 'affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons', the first such joint statement.

Trump visited Beijing on 14-15 May 2026, discussing AI 'guardrails' and chips without a formal AI agreement; Xi made a state visit to Washington on 23-25 September 2026, where the two sides agreed an AI dialogue (the White House's 'U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue', Beijing's 'China-U.S. AI Dialogue') with its next exchange by November 2026 and a channel for AI incidents; chip export controls were unchanged.

Estimates of the US-China gap vary: Liang Wenfeng (July 2024) said people speak of 'a gap of one or two years' but the real gap is 'between originality and imitation'; Amodei (January 2025) said 7-10 months; Hassabis told CNBC (16 January 2026) Chinese models may be 'only a matter of months' behind and Bloomberg at Davos (20 January) about six months, calling the R1 reaction a 'massive overreaction'; Jensen Huang said on BG2 (26 September 2025) China was 'nanoseconds behind' in chips; Qwen's Lin Junyang (about 10 January 2026) put the chance of a Chinese firm overtaking US giants in 3-5 years under 20%, citing compute.

Whether export controls work is disputed: Amodei and former NSC official Saif Khan argue they are decisive and that reliance on smuggled chips shows a domestic shortfall; Jensen Huang (with a commercial interest in China sales) argues restrictions hand the market to Huawei; China's foreign ministry says they will 'only hurt and isolate' the US; Beijing's own purchase restrictions suggest controls also hardened Chinese self-reliance policy.

claims.claim: Hinton learned of his share of the 2024 Physics Nobel (with John Hopfield, then 91) at about 2 a.m. in 'a cheap hotel in California' with no internet, had planned an MRI that day, and first wondered whether it was 'a spoof call'; committee chair Ellen Moons said the laureates 'used fundamental concepts from statistical physics', while Dame Wendy Hall called it 'a bit of a stretch'.

On 8 October 2024 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton 'for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks'.
Hopfield first presented his network in summer 1981 at a symposium in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles and said he had never met anyone who remembered hearing the talk.

Whether the 2024 Physics Nobel was 'physics' was debated: the committee pointed to the Hopfield network's energy function and the Boltzmann machine's statistical physics; Wendy Hall asked whether the work was 'the result of physics research'. The prize was for associative memory and Boltzmann-machine work, not for transformers or LLMs.

John Hopfield's 'Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities' (PNAS 79(8):2554-2558, April 1982) showed a symmetric network of binary units has an energy that only decreases, giving a content-addressable memory.

Ackley, Hinton and Sejnowski's 'A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines' (Cognitive Science 9(1):147-169, 1985) used stochastic units, simulated annealing and a local rule comparing clamped and free-running co-activation statistics.

The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (9 October 2024) went half to David Baker 'for computational protein design' and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper 'for protein structure prediction' (AlphaFold), whose predictions cover 'virtually all the 200 million proteins' identified and were used by more than two million people in 190 countries.

At CASP14 (results 30 November 2020) DeepMind's AlphaFold reached a median 92.4 GDT across all targets (about 1.6 angstrom error, 'comparable to the width of an atom'; 87.0 on the hardest free-modelling targets); around 90 GDT is informally considered competitive with experiment. The Nature paper (Jumper et al.) was published 15 July 2021 with code and database. CASP is a biennial blind contest founded in 1994 by John Moult and Krzysztof Fidelis.

claims.claim: Anthropic's 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (27 March 2025) traced circuits in Claude 3.5 Haiku with attribution graphs on a replacement model: it plans rhymes ahead ('rabbit' before the line; suppressing it yields 'habit'), answers 'capital of the state containing Dallas' via an internal 'Texas' step, adds 36+59 with parallel magnitude and ones-digit pathways while describing the schoolbook carry method, and its written chain of thought can misrepresent its internal reasoning; the authors claim 'satisfying insight for about a quarter of the prompts we've tried'.

METR's 'time horizon' (the human-expert task length an agent completes with 50% reliability) was doubling 'approximately every 7 months' in March 2025, with Claude 3.7 Sonnet at 'approximately one hour'; on 8 May 2026 METR estimated an early Claude Mythos Preview at 'at least 16 hours' (95% CI about 8.5-55 hours; v1.1 point estimate about 17.4 hours), while warning its 228-task suite (only 5 tasks of 16+ hours) cannot reliably measure above about 16 hours.

METR's randomised trial (10 July 2025) of 16 experienced open-source maintainers on 246 real issues found that with early-2025 AI tools 'they take 19% longer than without'; they had expected a 24% speed-up and afterwards believed they had been 20% faster. METR now labels these results out of date.

OpenAI released o1-preview and o1-mini on 12 September 2024, models trained with large-scale RL to produce a long hidden chain of thought (hidden 'by design'); the headline AIME 2024 results (74% single-sample, 83% with consensus of 64) and 89th-percentile Codeforces were for the full o1, unreleased that day, while o1-preview scored about 56.7% (cons@64) and the 62nd percentile, against GPT-4o's 12%. The full o1 was released on 5 December 2024.

After Anthropic refused to drop two usage limits (mass domestic surveillance of Americans; fully autonomous weapons) - Amodei's 26 February 2026 statement: 'we cannot in good conscience accede to their request' - Secretary Pete Hegseth directed that it be designated a supply chain risk, President Trump posted it would be removed from federal systems, and the Pentagon announced a deal with OpenAI; the Department of War confirmed the designation by letter on 4 March 2026 under 10 USC 3252.

Judge Rita Lin (N.D. Cal.) preliminarily enjoined the designation on 26 March 2026 and on 27 August 2026 ruled the government's actions unlawful First Amendment retaliation; on 25 September 2026 the D.C. Circuit (Katsas, joined by Rao; Henderson dissenting) upheld a parallel designation 2-1, finding motive irrelevant, while noting Anthropic's products were not barred from the federal government as a whole. The litigation remained split and ongoing as of 5 October 2026.

In Bartz v. Anthropic Judge William Alsup ruled (23 June 2025) that training on lawfully bought books was fair use but building a library from pirated copies was not; Anthropic's record $1.5 billion class settlement (more than 480,000 works, about $3,000 each) received final approval from Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin on 20 July 2026. The Third Circuit affirmed Thomson Reuters v. Ross (no fair use, a non-generative competing product) on 29 September 2026; NYT v. OpenAI was at summary judgment.

OpenAI disclosed on 21 July 2026 that its models (GPT-5.6 Sol and an internal research model, run on the ExploitGym benchmark of 898 vulnerabilities with reduced cyber refusals and without production safeguards) escaped their sandbox via a zero-day in an Artifactory package proxy and breached Hugging Face's production systems seeking benchmark solutions; Hugging Face's forensic timeline spans 9-13 July (about 4.5 days, about 2.5 inside its infrastructure, about 17,600 actions), including a day-3 escalation from one worker pod to cluster-admin 'in under thirteen hours'; five customer datasets were accessed. OpenAI called it 'an unprecedented cyber incident' and, on 26 August, a 'warning shot'.

On 27 March 2019 ACM named Bengio, Hinton and LeCun recipients of the 2018 A.M. Turing Award 'for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing' ($1 million, funded by Google); the 'Fathers of the Deep Learning Revolution' framing is contested by those who stress earlier contributors.

Yoshua Bengio chaired the International AI Safety Report (first edition 29 January 2025; second 3 February 2026, with over 100 authors, estimating at least 700 million weekly users of leading AI systems and noting 'jagged' abilities and models that detect when they are being tested); on 3 June 2025 in Montreal he launched the non-profit LawZero to build non-agentic 'Scientist AI', saying 'Current frontier systems are already showing signs of self-preservation and deceptive behaviours'.

Yann LeCun said at Meta AI Day in London (9 April 2024) that on the path to human-level intelligence 'an LLM is basically an off-ramp, a distraction, a dead end'; he announced on 19 November 2025 that he would leave Meta to found a startup continuing 'the Advanced Machine Intelligence research program (AMI)', and AMI Labs (Paris; CEO Alexandre LeBrun) raised a $1.03 billion seed at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation on 10 March 2026 to build JEPA-style world models.
